title: Growing and drying herbs at home
subtitle: From the garden to the jar
excerpt: How to grow the most useful herbs for home herbal medicine, when to harvest each part, how to dry them, and how to store them. Covers chamomile, lavender, calendula, lemon balm, thyme, sage, rosemary, and elderflower. After reading this, you will have a working kitchen herb store that you have grown and prepared yourself.
sourceNotes: Maud Grieve, A Modern Herbal (1931) : harvesting and drying notes throughout. RHS guidance on culinary and medicinal herb growing (published guidance, not cited as a body source). Juliette de Baïracli Levy, Herbal Handbook for Farm and Stable (original edition) : practical preparation methods for home-grown herbs. General drying-temperature guidance (35 to 40 degrees Celsius for dehydrator, warm moving air for bunches) is standard across British and European herbalism texts. Fresh-to-dried potency ratio of 3 to 5 times is a standard rule of thumb in herbal preparation literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: The process of removing moisture from plant material to halt decomposition and concentrate the active constituents. Properly dried herb retains its colour, scent, and potency for up to 12 months.

content.text: Growing and
drying herbs

at home: which herbs to grow, when to harvest each part, how to dry them, and how to store them. This is the practical guide for readers who want to source their own herbs rather than buy them in tins. After reading it, you will know which herbs are worth growing for home medicine, when the right harvest window is for each, and how to turn a fresh-cut bunch into a properly dried jar that will keep for 12 months.

This article does not cover identification of wild plants for foraging. For any herb you plan to harvest from the wild, use a field guide and confirm your identification before harvesting. For all the herbs in this article, cultivated garden or allotment growing is the practical and safe path.
The eight herbs worth growing

These eight herbs cover most of what a home herbal store needs. They are all straightforward to grow in the UK and in similar temperate climates, and they are all covered in more detail in their individual pages in this library.
Chamomile

German chamomile (Matricaria recutita) is an annual that self-seeds freely. Sow directly in spring, thin to 15 cm apart. The small white-petalled flowers with yellow centres appear from June. Harvest the flowers when the petals begin to reflexe (bend back from the centre): that is the peak of the volatile oil content. Pick in dry weather. Dry the flower heads on a single layer on a rack. They dry in two to three days in warm, moving air.
Lavender

English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) is a perennial shrub. Plant in a sunny, well-drained spot. Harvest the flower spikes just before they fully open, when about half the individual flowers are in bloom. Cut in the morning after dew has dried. Bunch ten to twelve stems together with a rubber band and hang upside down in a warm, airy room. Ready in seven to ten days: the stems should snap cleanly rather than bend.
Calendula

Calendula (Calendula officinalis, pot marigold) is a hardy annual that flowers from June to October if deadheaded regularly. Sow in spring directly in the bed. Harvest the fully open flower heads when the petals are fully spread and the resin on the back of the flower head is visible and slightly sticky. Pick in dry weather in the morning. Dry the whole flower heads on a rack; they take three to five days and shrink considerably as they dry.
Lemon balm

Lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) is a vigorous perennial. Harvest the young leafy tops before flowering, in June and July; the volatile oil content peaks before the plant directs energy into the flowers. Cut back by a third and the plant will regrow and give a second harvest. Dry in small bunches hung in a warm room, or on a rack. Lemon balm dries in four to seven days and the lemon scent should be strong in the dried herb.
Thyme

Common thyme (Thymus vulgaris) is a small perennial shrub. Harvest the young growing tips in spring and early summer before the plant comes into full flower. Cut about a third of the stems. Bundle and hang in a warm, airy place. Dry in five to seven days. Strip the dried leaves from the stems before storing.
Sage

Culinary sage (Salvia officinalis) is a perennial shrub. Harvest in late spring before flowering. The large leaves dry easily: hang bunches or lay leaves on a rack. Dry in five to seven days. Note the safety caution for sage: it carries a pregnancy caution at therapeutic doses and is traditionally used as a milk-suppressant at weaning. Culinary use in cooking is unproblematic.
Rosemary

Rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus) is a perennial shrub. Harvest young growing tips in spring and early summer. Hang in bunches or strip the leaves straight from fresh stems and spread on a rack. Rosemary takes five to seven days to dry thoroughly. The dried herb should be crisp and retain its strong resinous scent.
Elderflower

Elder (Sambucus nigra) is a shrub or small tree found in hedgerows and gardens. The flowers appear in flat-topped clusters (corymbs) in June. Harvest the whole flower heads when fully open and the scent is at its strongest. Pick away from roadsides. Spread the heads on a rack and dry in a warm, airy place for two to three days. The flowers are delicate and dry quickly. Strip the tiny flowers from the stems before storing; the stems have a slightly different taste.
Drying methods
Bunches hung upside down

The simplest method for leafy herbs and flower-topped stems (lavender, thyme, rosemary, sage, lemon balm). Tie small bunches of ten to fifteen stems with a rubber band, hang upside down in a warm, dry, airy room with good air circulation. Away from direct sunlight, which fades the colour and degrades aromatic oils. Ready when the stems snap cleanly and the leaves crumble easily between the fingers: typically five to ten days in a warm kitchen or airing cupboard.
Single layer on a drying rack

Better for flower heads that would be squashed in a bunch (chamomile, calendula, elderflower). Spread the flowers in a single layer on a clean mesh rack or drying screen. Turn them gently each day. Ready in two to five days. Flower heads should feel papery and light, not soft or damp.
Dehydrator

If you have a food dehydrator, set it to 35 to 40 degrees Celsius for herbs. Higher temperatures degrade the aromatic oils. A dehydrator on the correct setting dries most herbs in four to eight hours. The result is reliably dry herb, which is the main advantage if your kitchen is humid.
How to tell when the herb is properly dry
Three tests.
The crumble test: the leaves crumble easily between the fingers with a slight crackle. If they feel soft, pliable, or slightly sticky, they need more time.

The colour test: the herb retains most of its original colour. Chamomile flowers stay yellow-white. Calendula stays orange. If the colour has gone brown or grey, it dried too slowly or at too high a temperature.
The smell test: strong, true herbal scent. A faint, dusty, or musty smell means the drying has gone wrong or the herb has begun to degrade.
Storage

Store dried herbs in airtight containers, away from direct light and heat. Airtight tins or amber glass jars with tight-fitting lids are both good. Clear glass jars on a kitchen windowsill look decorative but degrade the herb within a few months.

Label each jar with the herb name and the harvest date. Dried herbs keep their potency well for 12 months from harvest. After that the volatile oil content drops and the medicinal preparation will be weaker, though the herb is not harmful. Replace the store each season from the fresh harvest.
Fresh versus dried: what changes

Drying removes the water content of the plant, which is typically 70 to 90% of the fresh weight. This concentrates the active compounds significantly. Dried herb is typically three to five times more concentrated by weight than fresh herb. This matters when you convert between fresh and dried in a recipe.

If a preparation specifies dried herb and you have fresh, use three to five times the weight. If it specifies fresh herb and you have dried, use a third to a fifth of the weight. All the remedy pages on this site specify dried herb amounts. If you want to use fresh herb from the garden, multiply the dried amount by three to five.

There is one important exception to this rule: infused oils. Fresh herb in oil introduces water that will cause the oil to go mouldy. For all oil preparations, the herb must be dried. If you want to use your garden herb in an oil infusion, dry it first before it goes in the jar.
